title_en: Wangari Maathai: The Woman Who Planted a Movement
title_ru: Вангари Маатаи: женщина, посадившая целое движение
description_ru: Как кенийский учёный и активистка превратила посадку деревьев в борьбу за права, демократию и землю, и стала первой африканкой с Нобелевской премией мира.
text:
In 1977, in the backyard of a modest house in Nairobi, a Kenyan biologist planted seven saplings to mark World Environment Day. It was an unremarkable ceremony, attended by a handful of women and a few curious neighbours. Nobody present could have guessed that the gesture would grow into a movement that has planted tens of millions of trees across Africa, toppled the plans of a dictator's favourite developers and earned its founder the Nobel Peace Prize.

Wangari Muta Maathai was born in 1940 in the highlands near Nyeri, in what was then British colonial Kenya. Her family were farmers, and as a child she fetched water from a stream that ran clear beneath a stand of fig trees. Local people considered those trees sacred, and no one cut them down. She would later reflect that traditional beliefs, which some outsiders dismissed as superstition, had in practice protected the landscape better than many modern laws.

Education was her escape and, eventually, her weapon. A brilliant pupil, she was selected for a scholarship programme that sent Kenyan students to the United States, and in 1960 she travelled to a Catholic women's college in Kansas to study biology. She went on to earn a master's degree at the University of Pittsburgh. Returning to a newly independent Kenya, she pursued doctoral research at the University of Nairobi, and in 1971 she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to hold a doctorate. She then rose to head the department of veterinary anatomy, again the first woman to do so.

Her academic success did not shield her from prejudice. Her husband, a politician, eventually divorced her, and a judge who sided with him reportedly accused her of being too educated, too strong, too successful and too stubborn to be controlled by any man. When she criticised the judge in an interview she was briefly jailed for contempt of court. She later wrote that the episode, far from silencing her, hardened her resolve and taught her that a woman who challenges the established order should expect to be punished for it, and should prepare accordingly.

The idea for her life's work emerged from listening. Rural women told her that streams were drying up, that firewood was growing scarce and that children were suffering from poor diets because the land around them was exhausted. Deforestation, soil erosion and poverty, she realised, were not three separate problems but one. The solution seemed disarmingly simple: plant trees. The Green Belt Movement, which began under the umbrella of the National Council of Women of Kenya, trained women to establish village nurseries and paid them a small sum for each seedling that survived. It gave them income, status and a sense that their knowledge mattered.

Over time the movement turned into something larger than forestry. Maathai started to teach civic education, explaining to villagers how their government worked and why their votes were important. For Kenya's autocratic president, Daniel arap Moi, whose party ruled for decades without serious opposition, an organised network of rural women who asked difficult questions was a threat, and he treated it as one.

The confrontation came into the open in 1989, when the government announced a sixty-storey skyscraper, with a statue of the president in front of it, in Uhuru Park, the largest green space in central Nairobi. Maathai wrote to potential investors, appeared on foreign television and filed a lawsuit. Officials mocked her as a hysterical woman and Moi called her ill-mannered and a threat to national order. Parliament members suggested that she was behaving in a way unbecoming of a woman. The foreign funding for the tower collapsed, and the park survived.

Victory carried a cost. She was harassed, arrested and, in 1992, beaten unconscious by police while protesting for the release of political prisoners. In 1998 she tried to stop the clearing of Karura Forest, which was being allocated to politically connected developers, and she was struck by guards armed with clubs. Photographs of her bleeding, but still defiant, were seen around the world. Each attack, ironically, strengthened her international reputation.

The political climate shifted at the end of 2002, when Moi's party lost power in Kenya's first genuinely democratic election in a generation. Maathai was elected to parliament with a staggering ninety-eight per cent of the vote, and the new president appointed her an assistant minister for the environment. Her record in government was modest, as she was frustrated by the slow pace of bureaucracy, but her stature was extraordinary.

In 2004 the Nobel Committee awarded her the Peace Prize, the first ever given to an African woman and the first awarded to anyone for work centred on the environment. Some critics wondered what trees had to do with peace. Her reply, delivered in Oslo, was characteristically patient: when resources are managed badly, she explained, people fight over what remains, and sustainable development, democracy and peace are inseparable.

Wangari Maathai died of ovarian cancer in September 2011, aged seventy-one. Her memoir, appropriately called "Unbowed", ends not with a triumphant flourish but with an invitation. She often told a story about a hummingbird that, when the forest was burning, carried tiny drops of water in its beak to the fire while larger animals stood by and watched. Told that it was too small to make a difference, the bird replied that it was doing the best it could. It remains a modest yet stubborn sort of heroism, and the forests she planted continue to prove that it works.

questions.question: What did the Green Belt Movement do for rural women?
questions.answer: Trained them to run tree nurseries and paid them for each seedling that survived.

questions.question: Why did she protest in Uhuru Park in 1989?
questions.answer: To stop a huge skyscraper being built in the park.

questions.question: What was historic about her 2004 Nobel Peace Prize?
questions.answer: She was the first African woman to win it.
